ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: Venus and Earth revolve around the Sun in the same plane, and both orbital paths are regarded as circular. As shown in the figure, when observed from Earth, it is found that the viewing angle that Venus and the Sun can present (the Sun and Venus are both regarded as point masses, and the angle between the lines connecting them with the eye) has a maximum value. If the sine value of this maximum viewing angle is n, then how can the orbital period of Venus be expressed?

As shown in the figure, when observed from Earth, it is found that the viewing angle that Venus and the Sun can present (the Sun and Venus are both regarded as point masses, and the angle between the lines connecting them with the eye) has a maximum value. ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: Venus and Earth revolve around the Sun in the same plane, and both orbital paths are regarded as circular. As shown in the figure, when observed from Earth, it is found that the viewing angle that Venus and the Sun can present (the Sun and Venus are both regarded as point masses, and the angle between the lines connecting them with the eye) has a maximum value. If the sine value of this maximum viewing angle is n, then how can the orbital period of Venus be expressed?
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, the Sun is marked near the center, and there are two circular orbits centered on the Sun around it; Venus is located on the inner circular orbit, and Earth is located on the outer circular orbit, conforming to the schematic of Venus and Earth moving in circular motion around the Sun in the same plane. Reasoning: Let the radius of Earth's orbit be R, and the radius of Venus's orbit be r. The viewing angle of the Sun and Venus observed from Earth is the angle formed by Sun—Earth—Venus. For an inner planet, the maximum viewing angle occurs when the line of sight from Earth to Venus is tangent to Venus's circular orbit. At this time, the Sun, Venus, and Earth form a right triangle, with the right angle at Venus. If the maximum viewing angle is α, then in this right triangle sin α = opposite side/hypotenuse = r/R. The problem gives sin α = n, so r/R = n. By Kepler's third law T^2 ∝ a^3, taking Earth's orbital period as 1 year, the Venus period T_V = (r/R)^{3/2} = n^{3/2} = \sqrt{n^3}.
